claim: The six-subunit Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) is believed to be an essential eukaryotic ATPase that binds to origins of replication as a ring-shaped heterohexamer to load MCM2-7 and initiate DNA replication.
source: The six-subunit Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) is believed to be an essential eukaryotic ATPase that binds to origins of replication as a ring-shaped heterohexamer to load MCM2-7 and initiate DNA replication.
evidence: This represents established scientific consensus about ORC function in DNA replication.

claim: Human cell lines in culture proliferate with intact chromosomal origins of replication after disruption of both alleles of ORC2.
source: We have discovered that human cell lines in culture proliferate with intact chromosomal origins of replication after disruption of both alleles of ORC2 or of the ATPase subunit, ORC1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cell proliferation and origin mapping in ORC2-/- cells.

claim: Human cell lines in culture proliferate with intact chromosomal origins of replication after disruption of both alleles of ORC1.
source: We have discovered that human cell lines in culture proliferate with intact chromosomal origins of replication after disruption of both alleles of ORC2 or of the ATPase subunit, ORC1.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing cell proliferation and origin mapping in ORC1-/- cells.

claim: ORC1 or ORC2-depleted cells replicate with decreased chromatin loading of MCM2-7.
source: The ORC1 or ORC2-depleted cells replicate with decreased chromatin loading of MCM2-7 and become critically dependent on another ATPase, CDC6, for survival and DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figures 1H and 3D.

claim: ORC1 or ORC2-depleted cells become critically dependent on CDC6 for survival and DNA replication.
source: The ORC1 or ORC2-depleted cells replicate with decreased chromatin loading of MCM2-7 and become critically dependent on another ATPase, CDC6, for survival and DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that CDC6 knockdown severely affects ORC1-/- and ORC2-/- cells but not WT cells.

claim: The ORC ring lacking a subunit, even its ATPase subunit, can load enough MCM2-7 in partnership with CDC6 to initiate DNA replication.
source: Thus, either the ORC ring lacking a subunit, even its ATPase subunit, can load enough MCM2-7 in partnership with CDC6 to initiate DNA replication, or cells have an ORC-independent, CDC6-dependent mechanism to load MCM2-7 on origins of replication
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: Cells have an ORC-independent, CDC6-dependent mechanism to load MCM2-7 on origins of replication.
source: Thus, either the ORC ring lacking a subunit, even its ATPase subunit, can load enough MCM2-7 in partnership with CDC6 to initiate DNA replication, or cells have an ORC-independent, CDC6-dependent mechanism to load MCM2-7 on origins of replication
evidence: This is a speculative alternative interpretation of the experimental findings.

claim: ORC is an essential six-subunit, ring-shaped ATPase complex that recruits and co-operates with the CDC6 protein to promote the loading of CDT1 and then the MCM2-7 subunits of the replicative helicase during the 'licensing' of origins of replication.
source: ORC is an essential six-subunit, ring-shaped ATPase complex that recruits and co-operates with the CDC6 protein to promote the loading of CDT1 and then the MCM2-7 subunits of the replicative helicase during the 'licensing' of origins of replication (Bleichert et al., 2015; Yeeles et al., 2015; Bell and Stillman, 1992; Blow and Tada, 2000; Masai et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ORC2-5 form a tight core complex of human ORC.
source: Of the six subunits of human ORC, ORC2-5 form a tight core complex (Dhar et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: ORC1 is the only subunit responsible for the ATPase activity of ORC.
source: ORC1 is the only subunit responsible for the ATPase activity of ORC (Chesnokov et al., 2001; Giordano-Coltart et al., 2005; Klemm et al., 1997)
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: All six ORC subunit genes are essential for the viability of S. cerevisiae and S. pombe.
source: All six ORC subunit genes are essential for the viability of S. cerevisiae and S. pombe (Bell et al., 1993; Foss et al., 1993; Herskowitz, 1993; Loo et al., 1995; Micklem et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A ~600 bp blasticidin gene and poly A site was inserted into exon 4 (amino acid 40) of ORC2 in HCT116 p53-/- colon cancer cells using CRISPR/Cas9.
source: CRISPR/Cas9 was used to insert a ~600 bp blasticidin gene and poly A site into exon 4 (amino acid 40) of ORC2 in HCT116 p53-/- (Bunz et al., 1998) colon cancer cells (WT: HCT116 p53-/-, ORC2+/+) (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: All clones with disrupted ORC2 gene were viable and proliferated for months.
source: All clones were viable and proliferated for months despite the disruption of the ORC2 gene.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation of cell viability and proliferation.

claim: ORC2-/- B2 and BP8 clones had no detectable ORC2 protein by immunoblotting and immunoprecipitation-immunoblotting.
source: Immunoblotting and immunoprecipitation-immunoblotting of cell extracts showed that the ORC2-/- B2 and BP8 clones had no detectable ORC2 protein (Figure 1D–H).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D-H.

claim: A C-terminal fragment of ORC2 was not being expressed from an alternatively spliced transcript using an internal methionine in ORC2-/- cells.
source: An anti-ORC2C antibody recognizing the C terminal half of ORC2 (Figure 1C) ensured that a C-terminal fragment of ORC2 was not being expressed from an alternatively spliced transcript using an internal methionine (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1E.

claim: If any ORC2 was expressed in B2 or BP8 clones, it must be at a level <1% of wild type levels.
source: Quantitative immunoblotting showed that if any ORC2 was expressed, it must be at a level <1% of wild type levels (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Wild type cells express ~153,000 ORC2 molecules per cell.
source: Quantitative immunoblotting of cell lysates and carefully measured amounts of recombinant bacterially produced ORC2 fragment showed that wild type cells express ~153,000 ORC2 molecules per cell (Figure 1I,J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1I and J.

claim: If the B2 or BP8 clones contain any ORC2 molecules below the level of detection, they can have no more than 1530 molecules/cell.
source: Thus, if the B2 or BP8 clones contain any ORC2 molecules below the level of detection, they can have no more than 1530 molecules/cell.
evidence: This is inferred from the <1% detection limit and the 153,000 molecules/cell in WT cells.

claim: ORC2 was deleted in 293T human embryonic kidney cells and these cells continued proliferating in the absence of ORC2 protein.
source: ORC2 was also deleted in 293T human embryonic kidney cells or HBEC human bronchial epithelial cells immortalized with CDK4 and hTERT, and these cells too continued proliferating in the absence of ORC2 protein (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: ORC2 was deleted in HBEC human bronchial epithelial cells immortalized with CDK4 and hTERT and these cells continued proliferating in the absence of ORC2 protein.
source: ORC2 was also deleted in 293T human embryonic kidney cells or HBEC human bronchial epithelial cells immortalized with CDK4 and hTERT, and these cells too continued proliferating in the absence of ORC2 protein (Figure 1K).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1K.

claim: ORC2-/- cells suffer a decrease of ORC3, ORC4 and ORC5, which are destabilized when not complexed with ORC2.
source: The ORC2-/- cells suffer a decrease of ORC3, ORC4 and ORC5, which are destabilized when not complexed with ORC2 (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G and inferred from the known complex formation.

claim: ORC1 was decreased in ORC2-/- cells.
source: ORC1 was also decreased, but ORC6, CDC6 and CDT1 were unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: ORC6, CDC6 and CDT1 were unchanged in ORC2-/- cells.
source: ORC1 was also decreased, but ORC6, CDC6 and CDT1 were unchanged.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: There was no activation of the DNA damage checkpoint in ORC2-/- cells, measured by the phosphorylation of Chk1 or H2AX.
source: There was no activation of the DNA damage checkpoint, measured by the phosphorylation of Chk1 or H2AX, as would have occurred with impaired DNA replication.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Chromatin association of ORC2-5 and of ORC1 was decreased in ORC2-/- cells.
source: Chromatin association of ORC2-5 and of ORC1 was decreased in ORC2-/- cells (as expected from the decrease of these proteins in cell lysates) (Figure 1H).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The chromatin association of MCM3, 5 and 7 of the MCM2-7 was reduced, but not completely eliminated in ORC2-/- cells.
source: The chromatin association of MCM3, 5 and 7 of the MCM2-7 was reduced, but not completely eliminated.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: Chromatin association of ORC6 or CDT1 was relatively unchanged in ORC2-/- cells.
source: Surprisingly, chromatin association of ORC6 or CDT1 was relatively unchanged, while CDC6 association was slightly increased.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: CDC6 chromatin association was slightly increased in ORC2-/- cells.
source: Surprisingly, chromatin association of ORC6 or CDT1 was relatively unchanged, while CDC6 association was slightly increased.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 1H.

claim: The proliferation rate of the ORC2-/- cells was >50% that of WT cells.
source: The proliferation rate of the ORC2-/- cells was >50% that of WT cells (Figure 2A) and ORC2 did not re-appear even after passage of the cells for over a year.
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: ORC2 did not re-appear in ORC2-/- cells even after passage of the cells for over a year.
source: The proliferation rate of the ORC2-/- cells was >50% that of WT cells (Figure 2A) and ORC2 did not re-appear even after passage of the cells for over a year.
evidence: This is supported by experimental observation over extended culture time.

claim: ORC2-/- cells did not accumulate in S phase.
source: The ORC2-/- cells did not accumulate in S phase (Figure 2B) and completed DNA replication after release from an early S-phase block in the same time as WT cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: ORC2-/- cells completed DNA replication after release from an early S-phase block in the same time as WT cells.
source: The ORC2-/- cells did not accumulate in S phase (Figure 2B) and completed DNA replication after release from an early S-phase block in the same time as WT cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle progression data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The percentage of cells synthesizing DNA during a 30 min pulse was not significantly decreased in ORC2-/- cells.
source: The percentage of cells synthesizing DNA during a 30 min pulse was not significantly decreased (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: By molecular combing the median distance between bi-directional origins of replication in ORC2-/- cells was marginally increased to 113–118 kb from 96 kb.
source: By molecular combing the median distance between bi-directional origins of replication in ORC2-/- cells was marginally increased to 113–118 kb from 96 kb and the fork progression rate was slightly increased to 1.3–1.5 kb/min from 1.2 kb/min (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by molecular combing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The fork progression rate in ORC2-/- cells was slightly increased to 1.3–1.5 kb/min from 1.2 kb/min.
source: By molecular combing the median distance between bi-directional origins of replication in ORC2-/- cells was marginally increased to 113–118 kb from 96 kb and the fork progression rate was slightly increased to 1.3–1.5 kb/min from 1.2 kb/min (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by molecular combing data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: The ORC2-/- cells fire about 52,000 origins of replication.
source: Given the total DNA content of six billion bp in these cells, this measurement suggests that the ORC2-/- cells fire about 52,000 origins of replication.
evidence: This is inferred from the inter-origin distance measured by molecular combing and the total DNA content.

claim: ~13,000 BrIPseq origins were mapped to unique DNA sequence in the ORC2-/- cells compared to ~20,000 in WT cells.
source: ~13,000 BrIPseq origins were mapped to unique DNA sequence in the ORC2-/- cells compared to ~20,000 in WT cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Taking into consideration repetitive DNA and the diploid nature of the human genome, BrIP-seq suggests that about 52,000 origins are fired in the ORC2-/- cells.
source: Taking into consideration repetitive DNA and the diploid nature of the human genome, this method also suggests that about 52,000 origins are fired in the ORC2-/- cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the BrIP-seq data accounting for repetitive DNA and diploidy.

claim: 40% of the BrIP-seq peaks in ORC2-/- cells overlapped with that in WT cells.
source: 40% of the BrIP-seq peaks in ORC2-/- cells overlapped with that in WT cells, comparable to the overlap reported among origins mapped by different groups (Karnani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The <100% overlap of BrIP-seq peaks is explained by plasticity of origin usage.
source: The <100% of overlap is explained by plasticity of origin usage (Cadoret et al., 2008).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The inter-origin distances for the BrIPseq origins in ORC2-/- cells (26 kb) were slightly longer than in the WT (25 kb) cells (P value ~4.3e-07).
source: The inter-origin distances for the BrIPseq origins in ORC2-/- cells (26 kb) were slightly longer than in the WT (25 kb) cells (P value ~4.3e-07, Wilcoxon rank sum test) and the chromosome-by-chromosome distribution of inter-origin distances was similar to that in WT cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The chromosome-by-chromosome distribution of inter-origin distances in ORC2-/- cells was similar to that in WT cells.
source: The inter-origin distances for the BrIPseq origins in ORC2-/- cells (26 kb) were slightly longer than in the WT (25 kb) cells (P value ~4.3e-07, Wilcoxon rank sum test) and the chromosome-by-chromosome distribution of inter-origin distances was similar to that in WT cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The 4-fold shorter inter-origin distance in a population-based approach of origin mapping (BrIPseq) compared to molecular combing is due to the plasticity of origin usage.
source: The 4-fold shorter inter-origin distance in a population-based approach of origin mapping (BrIPseq) compared to molecular combing is also due to the plasticity of origin usage: only one out of four possible origins in a single DNA segment fire in one S phase, while all four origins are used in the entire population of cells (see discussion in Karnani et al., 2010).
evidence: This is inferred from the data and supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Origins are enriched in gene-rich domains and near transcription start sites in ORC2-/- cells.
source: Origins are enriched in gene-rich domains and near transcription start sites (Figure 2H and I) as reported in previous studies (Karnani et al., 2010; Cadoret et al., 2008; Danis et al., 2004; MacAlpine et al., 2004; Mesner et al., 2011; Sequeira-Mendes et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data shown in Figure 2H and I and citations to prior research.

claim: A blasticidin or a plasmid-derived DNA fragment was inserted in exon 1 of ORC1 at the initiator methionine.
source: A blasticidin or a plasmid-derived DNA fragment was inserted in exon 1 of ORC1 at the initiator methionine (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: Western blotting and immunoprecipitation-western blotting showed no ORC1 protein in the ORC1-/- clones.
source: Western blotting and immunoprecipitation-western blotting of ORC1 protein showed no ORC1 protein in the ORC1-/- clones (Figure 3C–E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: ORC1 depletion did not decrease ORC2, ORC3, ORC4, ORC5, ORC6, CDT1, and CDC6.
source: ORC1 is loosely associated with the other subunits of ORC, and unlike ORC2, ORC1 depletion did not decrease ORC2, ORC3, ORC4, ORC5, ORC6, CDT1, and CDC6 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Although ORC1 was absent, the remaining five subunits of ORC along with CDC6 and CDT1 could associate with chromatin in ORC1-/- cells.
source: Although ORC1 was absent, the remaining five subunits of ORC along with CDC6 and CDT1 (at least in one clone) could associate with chromatin.
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The chromatin loading of MCM3, 5, and 7 subunits of MCM2-7 is significantly decreased in ORC1-/- cells.
source: However, the chromatin loading of MCM3, 5, and 7 subunits of MCM2-7 is significantly decreased (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: At early passage (at one month), the ORC1-/- clones proliferated at 10–20% of the rate of WT cells.
source: At early passage (at one month), the ORC1-/- clones proliferated at 10–20% of the rate of WT cells but by 6 months of passage, their proliferation rates at about 50% of WT cells without reappearance of ORC1 protein (Figures 4A and 3E).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: By 6 months of passage, ORC1-/- clones proliferated at about 50% of WT cells without reappearance of ORC1 protein.
source: At early passage (at one month), the ORC1-/- clones proliferated at 10–20% of the rate of WT cells but by 6 months of passage, their proliferation rates at about 50% of WT cells without reappearance of ORC1 protein (Figures 4A and 3E).
evidence: This is supported by proliferation assay data shown in Figure 4A and western blot data in Figure 3E.

claim: ORC1-/- cells did not accumulate in S phase.
source: The cells did not accumulate in S phase (Figure 4B) and passage through S phase was not slowed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Passage through S phase was not slowed in ORC1-/- cells.
source: The cells did not accumulate in S phase (Figure 4B) and passage through S phase was not slowed (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by cell cycle progression data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: By molecular combing, inter origin distance in ORC1-/- cells was unchanged or slightly decreased.
source: By molecular combing, inter origin distance in ORC1-/- cells was unchanged or slightly decreased (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by molecular combing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fork progression in ORC1-/- cells was decreased to 0.8–1.0 kb/min from 1.2 kb /min.
source: Fork progression was decreased to 0.8–1.0 kb/min from 1.2 kb /min.
evidence: This is supported by molecular combing data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: BrIPseq analysis showed that the ORC1-/- cells fire ~13,000 unique origins, with 43% of them overlapping with origins in WT cells.
source: BrIPseq analysis showed that the ORC1-/- cells fire ~13,000 unique origins, with 43% of them overlapping with origins in WT cells (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The distribution of inter-origin distances between chromosomes in ORC1-/- cells was similar to that of WT cells or ORC2-/- cells.
source: The distribution of inter-origin distances between chromosomes, enrichment of origins in gene-rich segments and near transcription start sites was similar to that of WT cells or ORC2-/- cells (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Enrichment of origins in gene-rich segments in ORC1-/- cells was similar to that of WT cells or ORC2-/- cells.
source: The distribution of inter-origin distances between chromosomes, enrichment of origins in gene-rich segments and near transcription start sites was similar to that of WT cells or ORC2-/- cells (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Enrichment of origins near transcription start sites in ORC1-/- cells was similar to that of WT cells or ORC2-/- cells.
source: The distribution of inter-origin distances between chromosomes, enrichment of origins in gene-rich segments and near transcription start sites was similar to that of WT cells or ORC2-/- cells (Figure 4F–H).
evidence: This is supported by BrIP-seq data shown in Figure 4F-H.

claim: Knocking down CDC6 in WT cells did not decrease the % of cells in active S phase.
source: Knocking down CDC6 in WT cells (Figure 5A) did not decrease either the % of cells in active S phase (Figure 5B) or colony formation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knocking down CDC6 in WT cells did not decrease colony formation.
source: Knocking down CDC6 in WT cells (Figure 5A) did not decrease either the % of cells in active S phase (Figure 5B) or colony formation (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells increased phosphoChk2, suggesting the activation of DNA damage checkpoints.
source: In contrast, knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells increased phosphoChk2, suggesting the activation of DNA damage checkpoints indicating problems in S phase (Figure 5A), decreased actively replicating cells, and decreased colony formation (Figure 5B–C), suggesting that CDC6 becomes more important for DNA replication and cell proliferation in the absence of ORC2 or ORC1.
evidence: This is supported by western blot data shown in Figure 5A and inferred from the phosphorylation of Chk2.

claim: Knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells decreased actively replicating cells.
source: In contrast, knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells increased phosphoChk2, suggesting the activation of DNA damage checkpoints indicating problems in S phase (Figure 5A), decreased actively replicating cells, and decreased colony formation (Figure 5B–C), suggesting that CDC6 becomes more important for DNA replication and cell proliferation in the absence of ORC2 or ORC1.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells decreased colony formation.
source: In contrast, knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells increased phosphoChk2, suggesting the activation of DNA damage checkpoints indicating problems in S phase (Figure 5A), decreased actively replicating cells, and decreased colony formation (Figure 5B–C), suggesting that CDC6 becomes more important for DNA replication and cell proliferation in the absence of ORC2 or ORC1.
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CDC6 becomes more important for DNA replication and cell proliferation in the absence of ORC2 or ORC1.
source: In contrast, knockdown of CDC6 in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells increased phosphoChk2, suggesting the activation of DNA damage checkpoints indicating problems in S phase (Figure 5A), decreased actively replicating cells, and decreased colony formation (Figure 5B–C), suggesting that CDC6 becomes more important for DNA replication and cell proliferation in the absence of ORC2 or ORC1.
evidence: This is inferred from the differential effects of CDC6 knockdown in WT versus ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells.

claim: Knockdown of ORC5 did not change the cell cycle profile in ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- mutant cells.
source: Knockdown of ORC5 did not change the cell cycle profile in ORC-/- mutant cells (Figure 5E), and in fact more severely repressed the % of actively replicating cells in WT cells than in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by FACS analysis data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Knockdown of ORC5 more severely repressed the % of actively replicating cells in WT cells than in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells.
source: Knockdown of ORC5 did not change the cell cycle profile in ORC-/- mutant cells (Figure 5E), and in fact more severely repressed the % of actively replicating cells in WT cells than in the ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Knockdown of ORC5 still inhibited BrdU incorporation in the ORC1-/- and ORC2-/- cells.
source: However knockdown of ORC5 still inhibited BrdU incorporation in the ORC1-/- and ORC2-/- cells.
evidence: This is supported by BrdU incorporation data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: It is unlikely that a single ORC complex can catalytically load thirty-five MCM2-7 hexamers distributed 100 kb apart over 3.5 Mb of chromosomal DNA.
source: It is unlikely that a single ORC complex can catalytically load thirty-five MCM2-7 hexamers distributed 100 kb apart over 3.5 Mb of chromosomal DNA.
evidence: This is inferred from the number of origins and the limited number of ORC2 molecules that could be present.

claim: The crystal structure suggests that ORC2-3-5-4-1 are arranged in a gapped ring with a central channel that is wide enough to surround a DNA double-helix.
source: The crystal structure suggests that ORC2-3-5-4-1 are arranged in a gapped ring (with a central channel that is wide enough to surround a DNA double-helix), and that later in licensing, CDC6 slips into the gap between ORC2 and ORC1 to close the gap.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from structural studies.

claim: Later in licensing, CDC6 slips into the gap between ORC2 and ORC1 to close the gap in the ORC ring.
source: The crystal structure suggests that ORC2-3-5-4-1 are arranged in a gapped ring (with a central channel that is wide enough to surround a DNA double-helix), and that later in licensing, CDC6 slips into the gap between ORC2 and ORC1 to close the gap.
evidence: This is based on knowledge from structural studies.

claim: The ORC-CDC6 ring is proposed to interact with the MCM2-7 ring end-on-end during the loading of MCM2-7.
source: The ORC-CDC6 ring is proposed to interact with the MCM2-7 ring end-on-end during the loading of MCM2-7 (Bleichert et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on a citation to prior research.

claim: Loss of one subunit in the five-membered ORC ring makes it difficult for the remaining subunits to form a ring large enough to surround a DNA double-helix in the same manner as wild type ORC.
source: Loss of one subunit in the five-membered ORC ring makes it difficult for the remaining subunits to form a ring large enough (i) to surround a DNA double-helix in the same manner as wild type ORC or (ii) to interact with the MCM2-7 ring end-on-end.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and the experimental findings.

claim: Loss of one subunit in the five-membered ORC ring makes it difficult for the remaining subunits to interact with the MCM2-7 ring end-on-end.
source: Loss of one subunit in the five-membered ORC ring makes it difficult for the remaining subunits to form a ring large enough (i) to surround a DNA double-helix in the same manner as wild type ORC or (ii) to interact with the MCM2-7 ring end-on-end.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural model and the experimental findings.

claim: Human ORC1 and ORC4 are the only subunits that have intact Walker A and B motifs.
source: Human ORC1 and ORC4 are the only subunits that have intact Walker A and B motifs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of ORC structure.

claim: Multiple groups have shown that the ATPase activity of ORC (in S. cerevisiae, in D. melanogaster and in H. sapiens) depends exclusively on the Walker A and B motifs of the ORC1 subunit.
source: Multiple groups have shown that the ATPase activity of ORC (in S. cerevisiae, in D. melanogaster and in H. sapiens) depends exclusively on the Walker A and B motifs of the ORC1 subunit, and that this ATP binding and hydrolysis activity is essential for ORC function (Chesnokov et al., 2001; Giordano-Coltart et al., 2005; Klemm et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: ATP binding and hydrolysis activity of ORC1 is essential for ORC function.
source: Multiple groups have shown that the ATPase activity of ORC (in S. cerevisiae, in D. melanogaster and in H. sapiens) depends exclusively on the Walker A and B motifs of the ORC1 subunit, and that this ATP binding and hydrolysis activity is essential for ORC function (Chesnokov et al., 2001; Giordano-Coltart et al., 2005; Klemm et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Any ATPase activity necessary for replication in ORC1-/- cells can be provided by ORC4 or CDC6.
source: Even if an altered or partial ORC is initiating replication, we have to conclude that any ATPase activity necessary can be provided by ORC4 or CDC6.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings that ORC1-/- cells can replicate.

claim: There is a report arguing that ORC1 is not essential for endoreplication in Drosophila, because ORC1-/- larvae still allowed endoreplication in salivary gland cells, with only a twofold reduction of ploidy.
source: There is a report arguing that ORC1 is not essential for endoreplication in Drosophila, because ORC1-/- larvae still allowed endoreplication in salivary gland cells, with only a twofold reduction of ploidy (Park and Asano, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: The classic model of replication initiation where ORC first associates with the DNA, helps load CDC6, which then helps load CDT1 and MCM2-7 may still be important for efficient MCM2-7 loading.
source: The classic model of replication initiation where ORC first associates with the DNA, helps load CDC6, which then helps load CDT1 and MCM2-7 may still be important for efficient MCM2-7 loading.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the model.

claim: Inefficient MCM2-7 loading, perhaps with the help of CDC6, is sufficient for replication initiation and cell survival in the absence of six-subunit ORC.
source: The surprise is that inefficient MCM2-7 loading, perhaps with the help of CDC6, is sufficient for replication initiation and cell survival in the absence of six-subunit ORC.
evidence: This is inferred from the experimental findings.

claim: The six-subunit ORC does not appear to associate with chromatin as a holocomplex.
source: The other surprise is that the six-subunit ORC does not appear to associate with chromatin as a holocomplex.
evidence: This is inferred from the chromatin association data showing independent loading of different ORC subunits.

claim: ORC6 associates with chromatin normally despite a decrease in ORC1 (in the ORC2-/- or ORC1-/- cells) or ORC2-5 loading (in the ORC2-/- cells).
source: Clearly ORC6 associates with chromatin normally despite a decrease in ORC1 (in the ORC2-/- or ORC1-/- cells) or ORC2-5 loading (in the ORC2-/- cells).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data.

claim: ORC2-5 loading is independent of ORC1 loading (in the ORC1-/- cells).
source: Similarly ORC2-5 loading is independent of ORC1 loading (in the ORC1-/- cells).
evidence: This is supported by chromatin fractionation data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The origin plasticity of eukaryotes is attributed to the loading of excess subunits of MCM2-7 on chromatin.
source: The origin plasticity of eukaryotes is attributed to the loading of excess subunits of MCM2-7 on chromatin.
evidence: This represents established scientific knowledge.

claim: The plasticity of origin usage persists despite a significant reduction in the association of MCM2-7 on chromatin in ORC1-/- or ORC2-/- cells.
source: It is thus also surprising that the plasticity persists despite a significant reduction in the association of MCM2-7 on chromatin.
evidence: This is inferred from the BrIP-seq data showing similar origin distribution patterns.

claim: The absolute requirement for six-subunit ORC for licensing bi-directional origins of replication can be bypassed in some cell lines.
source: In summary, we suggest that the absolute requirement for six-subunit ORC for licensing bi-directional origins of replication can be bypassed in some cell lines.
evidence: This is inferred from all the experimental findings showing cell survival and replication without ORC1 or ORC2.
